ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: The attached figure is a graph of electric potential energy Ep versus displacement x, with the vertical axis labeled Ep and the horizontal axis labeled x. The curve overall decreases from left to right; the Ep at x1 is higher than the Ep at x2. The slopes of the curve near the two points x1 and x2 are both negative, and the descent at x2 is steeper, that is, the absolute value of the slope at x2 is larger. Then reason: The particle is negatively charged, is subject only to electric field force, and moves along the positive direction of the x-axis. From the relation between force and potential energy Fx = -dEp/dx, it can be known that in the figure dEp/dx < 0, so Fx > 0, and the direction of the electric field force is along +x. The displacement of the particle from x1 to x2 is also along +x, so the electric field force does positive work, and A is correct. Since q < 0, and F = qE, the direction of the electric field strength E is opposite to the direction of the electric field force F, and should be along -x, so B is wrong. The magnitude of the electric field strength |E| = |F|/|q| = |dEp/dx|/|q|. In the figure, the absolute value of the slope at x2 is greater than that at x1, so the field strength at x2 is larger, and C is wrong. Also Ep = qφ, and q < 0; in the figure Ep1 > Ep2. After dividing both sides by the negative charge, the inequality sign reverses, giving φ1 < φ2. Therefore, the electric potential at x1 is lower than the electric potential at x2, and D is correct.

ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
First describe the image: The attached figure is a graph of electric potential energy Ep versus displacement x, with the vertical axis labeled Ep and the horizontal axis labeled x. The curve overall decreases from left to right; the Ep at x1 is higher than the Ep at x2. The slopes of the curve near the two points x1 and x2 are both negative, and the descent at x2 is steeper, that is, the absolute value of the slope at x2 is larger.
Then reason: The particle is negatively charged, is subject only to electric field force, and moves along the positive direction of the x-axis. From the relation between force and potential energy Fx = -dEp/dx, it can be known that in the figure dEp/dx < 0, so Fx > 0, and the direction of the electric field force is along +x. The displacement of the particle from x1 to x2 is also along +x, so the electric field force does positive work, and A is correct. Since q < 0, and F = qE, the direction of the electric field strength E is opposite to the direction of the electric field force F, and should be along -x, so B is wrong. The magnitude of the electric field strength |E| = |F|/|q| = |dEp/dx|/|q|. In the figure, the absolute value of the slope at x2 is greater than that at x1, so the field strength at x2 is larger, and C is wrong. Also Ep = qφ, and q < 0; in the figure Ep1 > Ep2. After dividing both sides by the negative charge, the inequality sign reverses, giving φ1 < φ2. Therefore, the electric potential at x1 is lower than the electric potential at x2, and D is correct.
